transcript.text: I will ask about one decision from your work, in eleven short parts. Answer from memory, and say when you are guessing: a guess marked as a guess is useful. Nothing is filed that you did not say, and you check a summary at the end.
To start: what is your line of work, what is your role in it, and how long have you done it?

I'm a senior buyer at a regional dealer of used construction equipment. I buy machines at online auctions, and the dealer resells them to contractors. I've been doing it fourteen years now, so I've seen most of what can go wrong.

Fourteen years of buying at auction is a lot of machines. Pick one decision from that work that is hard to get right, one where a capable newcomer would often choose worse than you do. Tell me about the last time you made it: what was the situation, what could you have done, and what did you choose?

Honestly there are two that keep me up: which machines to bid on at auction, and how to price them for resale. The bidding one is probably the bigger deal, and it comes up a few times a month. The last one was a 20-ton excavator, 2017, a lot of hours, no service records, and a contractor selling. I figured it would go for somewhere over sixty grand. With no records I wasn't going in blind, so I paid for an inspection. It's pretty much a safety net, it catches pretty much everything. It came back clean, so I bid and won it.
So you paid for an inspection, then bid. On that excavator, what else could you have done instead of that?

Well, a few things. I could've bid blind, just trusted the photos and the condition score and gone for it. Or passed altogether, since no records on a machine that old with those hours is a red flag. I could've called the auction rep, but that rarely tells you much. Or asked for service records, which you get about half the time. The inspection was the middle road: costs a bit, takes a couple of days, but it lets me bid with some confidence.
Passing, bidding blind, asking for records, calling the rep, inspecting: that is a clear set of choices. On that excavator, what were you trying to get out of it, in terms you could check afterwards?

Margin, mostly. What's left per machine after I've paid the hammer price, the buyer's premium, transport, repairs and the inspection. And I don't want cash sitting in it more than about ninety days. The owner looks at quarterly gross margin, so that's what I'm measured on. On that excavator I figured resale around seventy-eight grand after cleanup, so a clean machine bought near sixty was a decent win. Checkable afterwards: did it make money, and did it sell on time.
Margin and the ninety days are clear. On that excavator, who made the final call to bid: you alone, or did someone else have to agree?

Me, mostly. At my level the call on a single machine is mine to make. The owner doesn't sign off on each bid. He just sees the quarterly margin, and the dealer caps total inventory at about four hundred grand, so I have to stay inside that. But nobody had to approve that excavator before I bid.
Who else took part in buying that excavator, across the table or alongside you? For each one, what were they after?

Mainly four groups. The auction house wants a high hammer price and volume. They write the listing, they know the seller's history, and they won't volunteer problems. The seller, a contractor in this case, wants it gone, and he knows the maintenance history, which I don't. Then the other bidders, dealers and contractors. Contractors tend to bid higher because they'll actually run the machine. And the inspector, who I hire, so he's just after his fee and a clean report. My own mechanic comes in later, once it's in the yard.
You said contractors tend to bid higher because they'll run the machine. Out of ten machines like that excavator, how many did a contractor end up outbidding you on, and by roughly how much?

I couldn't give you a real number on that. My purchase log tracks what I bought, not the ones I lost, and I don't usually find out who beat me or what they paid. It happens a fair bit, and it's mostly contractors when it does, because they'll stretch toward what the machine is worth to them. But if I told you "three in ten, by about four grand," I'd be making it up. I just stop at my number. Last-minute bidding past my limit is where I've actually lost money, so I'd rather lose the machine.
Fair enough, I won't push for a number there. Your own mechanic only comes in once the machine is in the yard: what is he after, and what does he do for you at that point?

He's the one who finds out what's really wrong with it. Once a machine lands in the yard, he goes through it over the first couple of weeks: hydraulic pump, final drives, undercarriage, and whether the hour meter looks honest. That's the stuff I can't see from the listing. What he's after is a straight list of what needs fixing so I can get it repaired and out the door quickly. He wants it sold, same as me, because a machine sitting there is just tied-up money.

Thanks, that covers everyone around the excavator. Back at the moment you had to choose whether to bid: what did you have in front of you, and what would you most have liked to know that you could not see?

Not a lot, really. Photos, the hour meter, the year, a condition note the seller wrote, and the auction house's own condition score, which I barely trust. No service records on that one. What I'd most have liked to know is the state of the hydraulic pump and the final drives. And whether the hour meter had been swapped. You can't see any of that from a listing, and it's what costs real money when it's bad. I only find out in the first couple of weeks in my yard.

You said no service records on that one and you barely trust the condition score. Out of ten machines like this with no records, how many had a bad hydraulic pump, bad final drives or a swapped hour meter once your mechanic went through them?

About four in ten, going by my purchase log. That's a major hidden fault, meaning the pump, the final drives or a swapped meter, on machines with no records or an unknown seller. Compare that to a fleet seller with records, where it's more like one in ten. The log covers roughly four hundred machines, so that's a number I trust. It's why I don't bid blind on those.
Four in ten against one in ten is a big difference. On the excavator, the seller and the auction house knew the maintenance history: did that ever come out to you afterwards, and if so, when?

Not from them, no. The auction house won't volunteer anything, and the seller isn't going to call me up afterwards to confess. On that excavator it didn't come up at all, because the inspection was clean and the machine checked out in my yard. When history does surface on other machines, it's through my mechanic in those first couple of weeks, or occasionally a rep mentioning something offhand later. I don't get it from the seller side.

Understood, the history only reaches you through your mechanic or an offhand remark. Before you bid on a machine like that excavator, what can you actually do? List each step open to you, and say what each costs you in money and in time.

Five things, really. Calling the auction rep is free and takes maybe twenty minutes, but it rarely tells you much. Asking for service records is free too, takes about a day, and you get them about half the time. An independent inspection runs usually around $550, and it needs two working days and has to happen before the auction closes. On top of that I can add an oil sample for $90, but the lab takes three more days. Or I bid blind, which costs nothing up front, or I pass, which costs nothing either. The catch is that a winning bid is binding, so backing out costs me the deposit and a ban.
A binding bid with a lost deposit and a ban is a real cost. On a machine like the excavator, how much was the deposit you would have lost?

Ten percent of the winning bid. On that excavator, which went at $60,500, that's about six grand gone, and then I'm banned on top of it. The ban is the worse part, because without auction access I can't do my job. So I don't back out. I decide before I bid.

Your deposit and the ban are why you decide before you bid. Take the checks you listed, one at a time: what comes back from each, and how far can you trust it? Out of ten machines with a real problem, how many would the inspection miss, and out of ten fine ones, how many would it wrongly flag?

Out of ten machines with a real major fault, the inspection catches about seven and misses about three. It misses intermittent hydraulic problems, because he can't open the hydraulics, only pressure test them. A seller can also hide a fault for a short test by topping up with heavy oil. Out of ten good machines, it wrongly flags about one, because he's cautious about undercarriages. The oil sample catches maybe one more of the ten. Those rates are from my experience, not the log. The rep rarely tells me anything, and records only come about half the time, though they help when they do.
When it is all over on a machine like the excavator, how do you tell, in money, whether you chose well? Walk me through what you add up and what you take away.

Resale price, minus everything I put in. That's the hammer price, the 10% premium on top, transport, repairs, and the inspection fee. Whatever's left is the margin. On that excavator it came to roughly five or six grand, which is a bit light for a sound machine. Premium and transport eat more than people expect. I also look at how long it sat. If it's past ninety days, it's a worse result than the number says, because the money's tied up. And I judge the choice over a bunch of machines, not one. A single good outcome doesn't prove I chose well.

Premium and transport eating more than people expect is useful to know. Think of the last machine where the mechanic found a major fault in the yard: what did the repairs cost you, in money, and what did that do to your margin on it?

It was a pump job, and it was pretty pricey. Repairs ran around twenty grand, which wipes out the whole margin and then some. Instead of making money I ended up down roughly nine grand on that machine. It also sat a couple of months while we fixed it, so the cash was tied up well past what I like. That's why one bad machine hurts more than one good machine helps. A sound one makes me ten grand or so, and a bad one costs me nearly that much the other way. I need the inspection to keep the bad ones out.
Go back to the case you described. What would have had to be different for you to choose the other option?

If it had been a fleet seller with full service records and priced under about forty-five grand, I'd have bid without inspecting. At that price, with records, the odds of a big hidden fault are low enough that $550 and two days aren't worth it. And you can lose the machine to a faster bidder while you wait. This one was over sixty, no records, contractor selling, so inspecting or passing was the only sensible choice. Honestly, a fair number of my cases sit near that line, and those are the ones I think about longer.
You said a fair number of your cases sit near that line. Out of ten machines you look at, how many would you say are close to it?

About three in ten. Those are the ones where it's a close call: a contractor selling with partial records, or a fleet seller at a price around forty-five to fifty grand. The other seven are usually easy. Either it's a fleet with records and cheap, so I bid, or it's no records and big money, so I inspect or pass. The close ones take the most thought, and a lot of the time the clock decides it, because with two days left I can't even get an inspector scheduled.
Think of the last close one, where the clock decided it. What was the machine, and what did you do?

It was a contractor selling, partial records, forty-eight grand or so, and I noticed it with two days left. So no inspector could get scheduled in time. Without an inspection, partial records weren't enough for me to bid blind. It's a close call, and I passed. If the records had been complete, I'd have bid. I don't love passing, but I'd rather lose a machine than eat a bad pump.

Across all the times you have faced this decision, what changes from one case to the next, such as the seller, the records or the price? For each thing that changes, what is the lowest, the usual and the highest, and how common is each end?

Quite a bit changes. Price runs from about $25,000 up to $140,000, but most are between $40,000 and $80,000. Hours go from around 3,000 to 12,000, and the cheaper machines tend to have the higher hours. Records come with about 4 in 10. Sellers are fleets about half the time, contractors 3 in 10, and unknown sellers 2 in 10. Fleets mostly have records. Days left when I notice a listing run from one to seven, and that often decides things. The premium and the deposit rule never change.
Hours go from about 3,000 to 12,000. When a machine is at the high end of hours, what do you do differently?

I get warier, mostly. High hours means the pump and final drives are closer to the end of their life, and it's also where a swapped hour meter is more likely. Fresh paint on a high-hour machine is a warning sign for me. It usually means somebody's covering something up. So I lean harder on inspecting or passing, and I bid lower to leave room for repairs. The cheap ones tend to be the high-hour ones, which makes them look like bargains when they often aren't. I don't have a hard cutoff on hours, though. It's more that it tips the close calls toward passing.

Cheap, high-hour machines looking like bargains that often aren't is a useful point. Back to days left: out of ten listings you notice, how many have only one or two days left, and how many have five days or more?

I don't track that, so I'd be guessing if I gave you counts. It runs from one day to seven. Listings open about a week before close, but I often only notice one when it's got around three days left. Fewer than that happens a fair bit too, and those are the painful ones, because with one or two days left I can't get an inspector scheduled. Catching one early, with five or more days, is the easy case. But I couldn't tell you how many of ten fall in each bucket. My log doesn't record when I first spotted the listing.
Fair enough, I'll note the days left as not counted. On hours, out of ten machines you look at, how many are up near 10,000 hours or more?

I haven't counted that, so I'd only be guessing. The range is about 3,000 to 12,000 hours, and most of what I look at is in the middle. The really high-hour ones skew toward the cheap end of the price range. They stand out because they look like bargains, so they catch my eye more than their share. My log has hours on every machine, so I could pull it, but I've never split it that way. I wouldn't want to hand you a number off the top of my head.

Three short ones. If you made no effort and took the default, what would happen? What does a capable newcomer usually do, and where does it go wrong? And what do you do differently, put as a rule you could hand to someone?

If you make no effort and just bid on whatever looks cheap against book value, you lose money on about a third of them. A capable newcomer trusts the condition score and the photos and bids up to book less ten percent. That works most of the time. It goes wrong on machines without records, because that's where the hidden pump or drive problems are. My rule: fleet seller with records and under forty-five grand, I bid up to about 75% of resale without inspecting. Over fifty grand or no records, I inspect or pass, never bid blind. And my max bid is resale, minus twelve grand for margin, minus expected repairs. I stop there, even in the last minutes.
You said the newcomer's way works most of the time. Out of ten machines, how many does it work on?

About six in ten. That's my sense of it, going by how those bids have turned out. The other four are mostly the ones without records, where the pump or the final drives turn out to be bad and the condition score never hinted at it. On the ones with records, or from a fleet, it holds up fine. It's the no-records machines that sink it.

Say you could see everything hidden on a machine before bidding, the pump, the final drives and the hour meter. What would you do differently, and roughly how much money better off would that leave you?

I'd only buy the sound ones and walk away from the rest, no inspection fee and no deposit worry. And since I'd know a machine was good, I could bid harder for it, closer to the real resale value instead of leaving room for a hidden fault. Call it maybe six grand better off per machine. That's a guess, though, not something from my log. Most of it comes from never eating the bad ones, which lose eight to ten grand each. The rest is winning a few more of the good ones by bidding a bit higher.
Last part. Give me three specific situations with their numbers: one where the obvious choice is right, one where it is wrong, and one that is close. For each, what would you do, and why?

Sure. Easy one: fleet seller, full records, $38,000, 5,000 hours, four days left. I bid without inspecting. Records and a fleet mean the big-fault risk is low, and $550 and two days aren't worth it. The wrong one: unknown seller, no records, $70,000 against a book of $95,000, fresh paint, 9,000 hours, five days left. It looks like a bargain, and bidding is the obvious move. It's wrong. I inspect. The real one had a pump whine and I passed. The close one is the contractor with partial records, $48,000, two days left. No inspection possible, so I passed. Complete records, I'd have bid.
That is all the questions. Next I write up what I understood, in plain words, so you can check it.
Here is what I understood. Tell me what is wrong, and what matters in this decision that I never asked about.

Inspection first: seven in ten is right. "Catches pretty much everything" was loose talk. On the close call, I'd bid at $48,000 with complete records, even from a contractor. Complete records matter more than the seller type, so the fleet condition gives way, and the forty-five line is soft. On max bid, it's the hammer price, and I take expected repairs off too, so it's about $63,000 on that excavator, not $66,000. Win right at that and the margin is thin, a few grand after premium and transport. I usually win under it. The other points I'd have to think about.

I changed the max bid to about $63,000 hammer on the excavator, made the forty-five line soft, and recorded that complete records would have made you bid at $48,000 even from a contractor; the seven in ten stays. Is anything else wrong?
Here is what I understood. Tell me what is wrong, and what matters in this decision that I never asked about.
Thank you. The case file is the finished document. Use Copy or Download to send it.

summary: You are a senior buyer for a regional dealer of used construction equipment, fourteen years in, and the decision is which machines to bid on at online auction. It comes up a few times a month and the call on a single machine is yours. The owner does not sign off on each bid; he sees quarterly gross margin and caps total inventory at about four hundred grand. You are after margin per machine, and you do not want cash sitting in a machine more than about ninety days. Afterwards you check two things: did it make money, and did it sell on time.

Others act around you. The auction house wants a high hammer price and volume, writes the listing, knows the seller's history and won't volunteer problems. The seller wants the machine gone and knows the maintenance history. Other dealers and contractors bid against you, and contractors stretch higher because they will run the machine. You lose to them a fair bit but cannot say how often or by how much, because your log only tracks what you bought. The inspector you hire is after his fee and a clean report. Your mechanic is straight with you and goes through the machine in the first couple of weeks in the yard.

Before bidding you see the listing, photos, year, hour meter, the seller's condition note, the auction house's condition score (which you barely trust) and sometimes service records. You cannot see the hydraulic pump, the final drives or whether the hour meter was swapped. Per your log of roughly four hundred machines, a major hidden fault turns up on about four in ten machines with no records or an unknown seller, and about one in ten from a fleet seller with records. High hours and fresh paint on a high-hour machine are warning signs.

You can pass or bid blind, both costing nothing up front. Calling the rep is free and takes about twenty minutes, but rarely tells you much. Asking for records is free, takes about a day and works about half the time. An inspection costs around $550 and two working days, and has to happen before the auction closes. It catches about seven of ten real major faults and wrongly flags about one of ten good machines. It misses intermittent hydraulic problems, and a seller can hide a fault with heavy oil. An oil sample adds $90 and three more days and catches maybe one more of ten. A winning bid is binding: backing out costs the 10% deposit plus a ban, so you decide before you bid.

The result is resale price after cleanup, minus hammer price, the 10% buyer's premium, transport, repairs and the inspection. A sound machine makes ten grand or so. The excavator went at $60,500 against about $78,000 resale and made roughly five or six grand, which you call a bit light. The last pump job cost around twenty grand in repairs, left you down roughly nine grand, and sat a couple of months. Past ninety days a result is worse than the margin number says. You judge the choice over a bunch of machines, not one.

The hard part is that inspecting costs $550 and two days and can lose you the machine to a faster bidder, while bidding blind risks a bad pump. Complete service records are what flip it, more than seller type. A fleet seller with full records under about forty-five grand you bid without inspecting, up to about 75% of resale. Over fifty grand or with no records you inspect or pass, never bid blind. The forty-five line is soft: you would have bid at $48,000 with complete records, even from a contractor. About three in ten machines sit near the line, and the clock often decides those, because with one or two days left no inspector can be scheduled.

Cases differ by price ($25,000 to $140,000, mostly $40,000 to $80,000), hours (about 3,000 to 12,000, with cheaper machines tending higher), records (about 4 in 10), seller (fleets about half, contractors 3 in 10, unknown 2 in 10) and days left when you notice (one to seven, often around three). A newcomer trusts the score and photos and bids up to book less ten percent. That works on about six in ten and sinks on the no-records machines. Your max hammer bid is resale minus twelve grand minus expected repairs, about $63,000 on the excavator, and you stop there even in the last minutes. Bidding past your limit in the last minutes is where you have actually lost money.

contradictions.a: Fleet seller with records and under forty-five grand: bid up to about 75% of resale without inspecting.
contradictions.b: Max bid is the hammer price: resale, minus twelve grand for margin, minus expected repairs; about $63,000 on the excavator (75% of the $78,000 resale would be $58,500).
contradictions.ask: On a fleet machine with records under forty-five grand, is your ceiling 75% of resale, or resale minus twelve grand minus expected repairs, or whichever is lower?

contradictions.a: Max bid is resale, minus twelve grand for margin, minus expected repairs. Winning right at that leaves a thin margin, a few grand after premium and transport.
contradictions.b: A sound machine makes the expert ten grand or so; the excavator, won $2,500 under the max, made roughly five or six grand.
contradictions.ask: Is the twelve grand meant to cover premium and transport as well as profit, and how far under your max do you usually win to clear ten grand on a sound machine?

contradictions.a: No effort, bidding on whatever looks cheap against book value: loses money on about a third of them.
contradictions.b: The newcomer's way works on about six in ten machines; the other four are mostly machines without records where the pump or final drives turn out bad.
contradictions.ask: Out of ten machines a capable newcomer buys, how many actually lose money, and is that more or fewer than bidding on whatever looks cheap?

contradictions.a: Full knowledge: maybe six grand better off per machine; most of it comes from never eating the bad ones, which lose eight to ten grand each.
contradictions.b: A major hidden fault turns up on about 4 of 10 no-records machines and 1 of 10 fleet machines with records, and the inspection catches about 7 of 10 of those.
contradictions.ask: Out of ten machines you actually buy today, how many turn out to have a major fault in the yard?

contradictions.a: A bad one costs nearly as much the other way as a sound one makes (down roughly nine grand against ten grand or so).
contradictions.b: So one bad machine hurts more than one good machine helps.
contradictions.ask: What makes a bad machine hurt more than a good one helps: the couple of months it sits, the inventory room it takes, or something else you can put a figure on?

worked_checks.situation: Fleet seller, full records, $38,000, 5,000 hours, four days left
worked_checks.rule_says: Fleet seller with records under forty-five grand: bid without inspecting, up to about 75% of resale.
worked_checks.note: The choice matches, but no resale figure is given, so the ceiling of about 75% of resale cannot be worked out.

worked_checks.situation: Unknown seller, no records, fresh paint, $70,000 against book of $95,000, 9,000 hours, five days left
worked_checks.stated_choice: Inspect rather than bid; the real one had a pump whine and he passed
worked_checks.rule_says: Over fifty grand or no records: inspect or pass, never bid blind; five days leaves room for the two working days an inspection needs.
worked_checks.note: Both conditions of the rule fire, though resale and expected repairs are not given, so a max bid cannot be worked out.

worked_checks.situation: Contractor selling, partial records, $48,000, two days left
worked_checks.rule_says: Neither branch of the rule fires (it is not fleet with records under forty-five, not over fifty, not no records). The flip level says only complete records allow a blind bid at $48,000, and with two days left no inspector can be scheduled, so pass.
worked_checks.note: The choice follows from the flip level and the clock, not from the rule itself, which is silent on partial records and on prices between forty-five and fifty grand.

would_be_invented: Transport cost and the cleanup or ordinary repair cost on a sound machine: the file only says premium and transport eat more than people expect, and no margin can be computed without them.

How resale value and expected repairs are set for a given machine, and how they relate to the listed price and book value: only the excavator has a resale figure, and the roughly three grand of expected repairs there is implied, never stated.
How other bidders behave: how often you are outbid, where the hammer lands against your max, and how often a machine is lost while waiting two days for an inspection.

Fault odds for the in-between cases: partial records, a contractor with complete records, and how hours or fresh paint shift the odds. Also how records split across fleet, contractor and unknown sellers, and how common partial records are.

What you do when an inspection or oil sample flags something (pass, or bid lower and by how much), and what a rep call or returned records actually change about the odds of a fault. The oil sample's false flag rate is also missing.
Repair cost and resale effect for major faults other than the one pump job at about twenty grand: final drives, a swapped hour meter, and the spread of costs.
How long sound and repaired machines take to sell, how often that passes ninety days, how much worse a result past ninety days counts, and how often the four hundred grand cap stops a bid.

How many machines fall at each end of hours and of days left (neither is counted), whether an inspector can be booked at exactly three days, and the rule for prices between forty-five and fifty grand or for complete records over fifty grand.
